The majority voted against a motion to amend the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html), which is that the majority should agree with the main idea of the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6256) (or, in parliamentary jargon, that the majority should agree to read the bill for a second time). Since this motion was unsuccessful, the original motion will remain unchanged and [can be voted on as is](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/representatives/2018-12-06/3). ### Motion text > *That all words after “That” be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *“the House declines to give the bill a second reading, and notes:* > *(1) this unprecedented intervention into markets which will result in higher prices for families and businesses;* > *(2) the Government has abandoned all pretence at being the party of free enterprise and open markets; and* > *(3) the Government has abandoned all proper process, scrutiny and consultation.”* ### What is the main idea of the bill? This bill is part of the Government's package of measures in relation to the electricity sector. For example, the bill sets out three kinds of prohibited conduct in relation to retail prices, the electricity financial contract market and the wholesale electricity market. The remedies included in the bill are graduated, from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) issuing a public warning notice to the ACCC applying to a court for a pecuniary penalty. The bill also gives new compulsory information gathering powers on the Australian Energy Regulator (AER) and lets the AER share information with other agencies. The Labor Party was concerned with the [speed this legislation](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2018-12-05.125.2) was being pushed through Parliament by the Coalition Government.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to resume debate on the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, arguing that passing it within 48 hours would allow Senate passage by February 2019 and force energy companies to lower electricity prices, while delay would push passage to at least April 2019.

The speaker argued that Labor opposes the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 to protect big energy company profits, citing an ACCC finding that three players control 80% of dispatchable generation. They claimed Labor's 45% emission reduction target requires higher electricity prices and will wreck the economy, also tightening rules on farmers' land.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, which creates prohibitions on retail pricing, contract liquidity, and wholesale bid misconduct to lower electricity costs. The bill establishes a graduated enforcement process—including warning notices, civil penalties up to $10 million or 10% of turnover, and divestment as a last resort—citing ACCC evidence of market dysfunction and price discrepancies such as $411–$832 annual differences for households.

The speaker argued that the government rushed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 through parliament without proper scrutiny, calling the process chaotic and unacceptable. They criticised the government’s energy policy as a "dog's breakfast" and "harebrained," noting it was the tenth iteration, lacked expert support, and included an unprecedented and possibly unconstitutional divestiture power not recommended by ACCC chairman Rod Sims.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, arguing that divestiture powers for the ACCC should extend to all markets, not just energy, to address abuses such as supermarkets squeezing agricultural suppliers. The speaker credited former senator Nick Xenophon for championing this power and noted that the court, not a minister, should have the final say on divestiture as a remedy of last resort.

The speaker argued the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 would penalise energy companies for misconduct with graduated penalties including divestiture, and criticised the Queensland Labor government for maintaining an effective monopoly, overinvesting $7.3 billion in poles and wires, imposing a six per cent guaranteed return, and failing to pass on a 40 per cent wholesale price reduction to consumers.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 was condemned as the worst, shallowest, and most ill-conceived legislation seen in the parliament, being rushed, unsupported by any inquiry or the ACCC, and opposed by business groups—argued to fail in reducing electricity prices, increase carbon emissions, deter investment, and destroy jobs.

The majority voted in favour of [government amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-11.4.2) (1) to (5) and (8) to (11), which means they succeeded. ### What do these amendments do? These amendments would move several matters that are currently in disallowable instruments - that is, legislative instruments that the parliament is able to vote against in a single vote so they stop being law - to standard legislation that can't so easily be undone. These matters include the location of the trial sites. According to Liberal MP [Mitch Fifield](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/mitch_fifield), who introduced the amendments, *"[this will give certainty](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-09-11.6.1) to trial participants and local communities"*. ### What does the bill do? The [bill was introduced to](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6130): * *expand the cashless debit card arrangements to a further trial site, the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay area, to run until 30 June 2020;* * *specify the class of trial participants for the area and increase the total number of trial participants overall to 15 000;* * *provide for an exception from the restrictive trade practices provisions of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 for merchants that implement product level blocking systems to identify that a cashless debit card is being used for payment and, if any restricted products are being purchased, decline the transaction; and* * *limit the use of the restricted portion of a payment to prevent the portion being used to obtain cash-like products which could be used to obtain alcohol or gambling.*
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Cashless Debit Card Trial Expansion) Bill 2018 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

Labor opposed the expansion of the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing community opposition from both local mayors, a lack of formal consultation, an inconclusive and poor-quality ORIMA evaluation, and program costs exceeding $24 million to date (including $7.9 million paid to Indue and $1.6 million to ORIMA). It committed to supporting the current trials in Ceduna and the East Kimberley until mid-2019, but would only consider new sites with credible evidence of effectiveness and an agreed community consultation process and definition of consent.

The speaker argued for the expansion of the Cashless Debit Card trial to the Hinkler electorate, citing strong community support, over 188 consultation meetings, a ReachTEL poll showing 27.8% opposition, and a cost of less than $2,000 per person. They invited the member for Barton to meet frontline service providers rather than union officials, and noted that the trial would affect 6,700 participants on specific welfare payments to address child neglect and gambling-related harm.

The speaker argued for expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing independent evaluation results showing reduced alcohol and drug use, gambling, and improved savings and childcare in existing trial sites (Ceduna and East Kimberley). The bill extends the trial to about 6,700 welfare recipients under 36 in those areas, with additional $1 million in community services, and amends the list of restricted goods to include cash-like products.

The member for Herbert opposed the cashless debit card trial expansion, arguing it should not be imposed on communities that reject it, and instead advocated for early intervention and prevention programs, citing a $5 million commitment to a Salvation Army detox facility and noting that 78% of trial participants reported little or no change.

The speaker opposed the bill to expand the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, arguing the government failed to properly consult communities and lacked credible evidence. They noted the expansion would add around 6,700 participants, bringing the total to over 15,000, and criticised the $1.6 million ORIMA evaluation as unreliable while highlighting the $24 million spent on existing trials.

The bill expands the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, covering around 6,700 people under 36 on Newstart, youth allowance, or parenting payments, running until 30 June 2020, based on community consultation and evidence of intergenerational welfare dependency.

The speaker argued against expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing a woeful evaluation, no reduction in violence, and a damning Auditor-General's report, while supporting continuation of existing trials in Ceduna and East Kimberley for two years. They opposed the national rollout, insisting on genuine community consultation and wraparound services instead of mandatory income management.

The majority voted to agree with [the bill's](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr5816%22) main idea. This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill was introduced to tighten the information disclosure requirements for the working holiday maker employer register. Firstly, it will ensure that details of the working holiday maker employer register will not be able to be made publicly available. Secondly, it'll ensure that information sharing between the Australian Tax Office (ATO) and the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) is only undertaken in situations in which an entity is non-compliant, or is reasonably suspected of non-compliance, with a tax law. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd088).

This means the Senate can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea?
